evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena scabra as native to the southern/central United States through Mexico and the Caribbean.
USDA PLANTS-derived county native-status data explicitly marks Verbena scabra native in Hays, Comal, and Travis Counties (and several other project counties).
The project Hays County native-source list independently includes Verbena scabra.
UT Plant Resources Center documents Travis and Williamson County material, providing supporting local occurrence/morphology context.
target_zone_range.guardrail: The strict decision relies on county records explicitly marked native in the USDA-derived dataset; broad southeastern U.S. range language alone is not used.

morphology.look_here_first: Feel or closely inspect the broad leaves: this is the big sandpaper-textured Verbena, with broad ovate leaves and long, thin flowering spikes that can form a branched panicle.
diagnostic_traits: broad ovate leaves, much wider than those of the other native B013 species
upper leaf surface harshly scabrous/sandpapery from short stiff hairs
lower nodes can root adventitiously in wet or submerged conditions
long slender spikes, often grouped into a branched panicle
flowers tiny relative to the very long spike
stems and rachises scabrous with pustulate-based hairs

confusers.separator: Both can become tall and branched, but V. scabra has much broader sandpaper leaves and very long slender spikes; Brazilian vervain has narrow simple serrate leaves and many short compact spikes in an open panicle.
V. xutha has distinctly lobed leaves and coarser discrete spikes; V. scabra has broad unlobed/serrate sandpaper leaves.
V. halei is much more slender with deeply divided lower leaves and narrow upper leaves.

installation_guardrail: Do not install until Calvin explicitly approves B013 pass taxa.
